name: Drostanolone

lead: Drostanolone, widely known as Masteron, is an injectable steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone. Bodybuilders use it as an add-on for a dry, hard, defined look when lean, and forum posters also discuss its effects on skin and hair.

It is a 2-alpha-methyl derivative of DHT, so it activates the androgen receptor and is not converted to estrogen by aromatase, which is why users link it to less softness and water. Medically it was tested from the 1960s to the 1980s as hormone therapy for advanced breast cancer. No study has measured its effect on physique, face or skin in healthy users.

paras: Users add it to a cutting phase alongside testosterone or other compounds, with a calorie deficit and training. The propionate ester is the usual injectable form, and users describe the look tightening over several weeks.

Breast-cancer trials judged side effects generally not serious in that setting. Forum users warn about hair loss in those predisposed, since DHT-derived compounds are not blocked by finasteride or dutasteride in their account, and about skin and cardiovascular effects of stacks. It is detected in anti-doping controls and prohibited in sport.

angle.text: Drostanolone (Masteron) is an injectable DHT-derived steroid that bodybuilders add during cuts to keep muscle and get a dry, hard, defined look. Human trials were in breast cancer; users also discuss its effects on hair and skin.

lead: Drostanolone, also called dromostanolone and best known by the brand name Masteron, is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone (DHT) with a methyl group added at the 2-alpha position. It is usually encountered as drostanolone propionate, an injectable ester [1][2][3].

In bodybuilding and looksmaxxing circles the appeal is appearance: users describe it as giving a harder, drier, more defined look when body fat is already low, and as a compound that adds muscle conditioning without being converted to estrogen, which proponents link with less water retention and with a sharper, more masculine look [4][5][2]. It is typically discussed as an add-on to testosterone or other compounds rather than a stand-alone product [6][5].

Medically, drostanolone propionate was used from the early 1960s to treat advanced breast cancer in women, under names such as Drolban and Masteril, and was studied in randomized trials from 1968 onward against oophorectomy, nandrolone, testolactone, ethinyl estradiol and tamoxifen [7][8][9][10][11][2][3]. It is no longer marketed for medical use [3].

No published study has tested drostanolone for cosmetic outcomes in healthy people. The human evidence consists of breast-cancer trials and anti-doping research, while community claims about physique, skin, hair and estrogen control come from user reports [7][12][11].
infobox: 1959; propionate introduced for medical use in 1961 [2][3]
US Schedule III; prohibited in sport; not currently marketed [2][3][13]

paras: Drostanolone propionate (Masteril) was tested in breast cancer in a trial from 1968 to 1972 against oophorectomy in premenopausal patients, nandrolone phenylpropionate in perimenopausal patients and ethinyl estradiol in postmenopausal patients; response rates were 44 percent versus 22 percent in the premenopausal group, 34.5 percent versus 39 percent in the perimenopausal group and 38.5 percent versus 57 percent in the postmenopausal group, and the authors described side effects as generally not serious [7].

Other randomized studies compared drostanolone with nandrolone, testolactone and testosterone decanoate, finding similar response rates, with added cyclophosphamide raising response rates in combination arms [8][9][10]. A 1982 French trial in 98 postmenopausal women found that hormonal therapy with tamoxifen plus drostanolone produced the best immediate objective responses and the fewest adverse effects compared with CMF chemotherapy or the combination [11]. Use declined as tamoxifen and later aromatase inhibitors became standard, according to Grokipedia, which also reports that the US approval was terminated in 1994 (a date the page itself gives inconsistently) [13].

In bodybuilding, drostanolone is associated with cutting phases, where users aim to preserve muscle and show conditioning as body fat falls; Wikipedia describes non-medical use for physique and performance enhancement, and Grokipedia says users favor it for muscle hardness and vascularity [2][13]. Users on a looksmax.org thread said it can look very good when lean [4].

Some forum users see it as relevant to facial masculinisation, arguing that DHT-type androgens support a more angular, masculine look [5]. Others ask whether it can be run alongside heavy skincare and retinoid routines to protect skin, and replies in that thread were mixed [6]. A fourth thread compared it with oxandrolone [14]. None of these claims has been tested in a trial.

Like other anabolic-androgenic steroids, drostanolone is an agonist of the androgen receptor. It is not a substrate for 5-alpha-reductase and a poor substrate for 3-alpha-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase, which Wikipedia says gives it a high anabolic-to-androgenic ratio (reported in rodents as roughly 1:3 to 1:4) [2]. The androgen receptor binds testosterone or DHT and regulates gene expression; in hair follicles DHT is the main androgen acting [15].

Because it is a DHT derivative it cannot be aromatized into estrogenic metabolites [2]. Grokipedia describes anti-estrogenic effects used historically in breast cancer; its actual effect on estrogen levels in users has not been shown in published trials [13]. It is not 17-alpha-alkylated, so it is not known to cause the liver toxicity linked with oral steroids, although Wikipedia notes that high doses or prolonged use could still harm the liver [2].

The propionate ester has near-zero oral bioavailability and is given by intramuscular injection; it acts as a prodrug and, per Wikipedia, has an elimination half-life of about 2 days [3]. Grokipedia gives 2 to 3 days and says metabolites leave mainly in urine as sulfate and glucuronide conjugates [13].

Drostanolone is 2-alpha-methyl-5-alpha-dihydrotestosterone (formula C20H32O2) [2]. Two crystal polymorphs of the propionate ester have been characterised by X-ray diffraction [1]. A methylated derivative, methyldrostanolone, has been identified in commercial products [16].

Drostanolone and its propionate were first described in 1959, in the same paper as oxymetholone and methasterone, and the propionate entered medical use in 1961, first in the United States and shortly afterward in Europe [2][3]. Grokipedia attributes development to researchers at Syntex [13]. Brand names over time included Drolban, Masteril, Masteron, Masterid, Permastril and others [3].

Clinical research in breast cancer ran through the 1960s to early 1980s [7][8][9][10][11]. After the drug left the medical market it continued to circulate through non-medical channels; Grokipedia says legitimate production had largely stopped by the late 1980s [13]. Surveys of competing bodybuilders in Flanders from 1988 to 1993 found 38 to 58 percent of controlled athletes positive for doping agents in some federations [17].

Clinical studies are limited to randomized breast-cancer trials from 1968 to 1982 comparing drostanolone propionate with oophorectomy, nandrolone, ethinyl estradiol, testololactone and testosterone decanoate, or combining it with tamoxifen or cyclophosphamide [7][8][9][10][11]. One 91-patient controlled trial compared testololactone, drostanolone and nandrolone in advanced breast cancer, recording remissions at 4 and 16 weeks [9]. A randomized comparison with testosterone decanoate and testololactone reported similar rates of objective response among the single hormone therapies [8]. No human study has examined drostanolone for appearance.

In breast cancer, randomized trials from the 1970s reported objective response rates of roughly a quarter to a half of patients depending on the comparison and whether chemotherapy was added, with no clear difference among the androgens compared [7][8][9]. No randomized trial has evaluated drostanolone for muscle, leanness, skin or facial appearance.

The breast-cancer trials reported that side effects were generally not serious and rarely contraindicated use in that setting [7]. Wikipedia lists virilization in women, acne, hair loss or accelerated male-pattern baldness, unfavorable cholesterol changes, possible liver damage and mood changes such as aggression and irritability [2]. Anabolic steroids as a class suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which can cause testicular atrophy, reduced sperm production and hypogonadism, raise blood pressure and LDL cholesterol while lowering HDL, and can accelerate pattern baldness in predisposed men [18].

Forum users cite hair loss in genetically predisposed people, and one stated that finasteride and dutasteride do not counteract DHT-derived compounds [4]. Another user reported only bloating and mood changes on a testosterone-based regimen without an aromatase inhibitor [5]. One forum user said it is known to be harsh on lipids, and another said strong androgens and DHT derivatives are associated with a "flatness" feeling [19][20]. In a T Nation thread about female use, a poster wrote that drostanolone induced low rates of virilization relative to testosterone propionate; the class as a whole carries virilization risk for women [21][2].

A study of hamsters found that animals self-administered drostanolone, along with nandrolone, oxymetholone and stanozolol, into the brain ventricles, work used to study the reinforcing properties of anabolic steroids [22]. Compounds sold as drostanolone on the gray market have been analysed for adulteration by NMR [23].

Drostanolone is one of the most frequently detected anabolic androgenic steroids in doping control analysis [12]. Urinary metabolites have been characterised for detection, including long-term metabolites [12][24][25][16], and Grokipedia lists WADA prohibition under S1 anabolic agents and several suspension cases in sport [13]. Forum members discussing natural bodybuilding contests list drostanolone among compounds banned by such federations [26].

In the United States drostanolone, like other anabolic steroids, is a Schedule III controlled substance; Grokipedia ties this to the Anabolic Steroids Control Act of 1990, lists it as Class C in the UK, and Wikipedia lists Schedule IV in Canada [2][13]. It is prohibited in sport [13][12].

On looksmaxxing forums, drostanolone appears in the stacks of young and adult posters and in debates over whether DHT-derived androgens help or harm facial appearance and hair [6][4]. Some members say they favor it over aromatase inhibitors for managing estrogen-related effects; others on the same thread recommend other compounds or say an aromatase inhibitor is rarely needed [5]. Members of the TRT-focused T Nation forum say some clinics add DHT-derived steroids such as drostanolone to testosterone regimens [27].

lore.intro: Drostanolone is discussed on looksmax.org and T Nation as a hardening, drying compound, as an estrogen-control add-on, and with recurring concern about hair loss and cholesterol [6][4][5][19].

claims.claim: Masteron gives a dry, hard, lean look.
Masteron can replace an aromatase inhibitor for controlling estrogen.
It may cause hair loss that finasteride cannot block.
Skincare and collagen products can offset the skin effects of a large steroid stack.
It is gentler on women because it virilizes less than testosterone.
It is hard on cholesterol and the heart.
